This ZIP (ZIP 226) proposes the Orchard Zcash Shielded Assets (OrchardZSA) protocol, in conjunction with ZIP 227
. The OrchardZSA protocol is an extension of the Orchard protocol that enables the issuance, transfer and burn of custom Assets on the Zcash chain. The issuance of such Assets is defined in ZIP 227

, while the transfer and burn of such Assets is defined in this ZIP (ZIP 226). While the proposed OrchardZSA protocol is a modification to the Orchard protocol, it has been designed with adaptation to possible future shielded protocols in mind.
This ZIP is defined relative to the Zcash protocol specification version 2026.8.0

None of the currently deployed Zcash transfer protocols support Custom Assets. Enabling multi-asset support on the Zcash chain will open the door for a host of applications, and enhance the ecosystem with application developers and Asset custody institutions for issuance and bridging purposes. This ZIP builds on the issuance mechanism introduced in ZIP 227
In order to be able to represent different Assets, we need to define a data field that uniquely represents the Asset in question, which we call the Asset Identifier
. This Asset Identifier maps to an Asset Base
that is stored in OrchardZSA notes. These terms are formally defined in ZIP 227
The Asset Identifier (via means of the Asset Digest and Asset Base) will be used to enforce that the balance of an Action Description
is preserved across Assets (see the Orchard Binding Signature

As was initially proposed by Jack Grigg and Daira-Emma Hopwood

as the base point in the value commitment
. This ensures (1) that the input and output notes are of the same Asset Base, and (2) that only Actions with the same Asset Base will balance out in the Orchard binding signature.

After the protocol upgrade, the Ironwood shielded pool will be shared by the Orchard protocol and the OrchardZSA protocol. The Orchard shielded pool cannot contain OrchardZSA notes.
Deploying the OrchardZSA protocol does not necessitate disabling the Orchard protocol. Both can co-exist and be addressed via different transaction versions.

The use of different value base points for different Assets enables the final balance of the transaction to be securely computed, such that each Asset Identifier is balanced independently, which is required as different Assets are not meant to be mutually fungible.

The burn mechanism is a transparent extension to the transfer protocol that enables a specific amount of any Custom Asset to be "destroyed" by the holder. The burn mechanism does NOT send Assets to a non-spendable address, it simply reduces the total number of units of a given Custom Asset in circulation. It is enforced at the consensus level, by using an extension of the value balance mechanism used for ZEC Assets. Burning makes it globally provable that a given amount of a Custom Asset has been destroyed. Note that the OrchardZSA Protocol does not allow for the burning of the Native Asset (i.e. ZEC or TAZ).

A Split Input is a copy of a previously issued input note (that is, a note that has previously been included in the Merkle tree), with the following changes:
The value of the note is replaced with the value 0 during the computation of the value commitment.
Input notes are sometimes split in two (or more) output notes, as in most cases, not all the value in a single note is sent to a single output.

When the number of input notes of a particular Asset Base is smaller than the required number of output notes for the same Asset Base, the sender creates Split Inputs of the same Asset Base as padding for the input-less Actions. Note that we do not care about whether the previously issued note copied to create a Split Input is owned by the sender, or whether it was nullified before.
Wallets and other clients have to choose from the following to ensure the Asset Base is preserved for the output note of a Split Action:
The Split Input note could be another note containing the same Asset Base that is being spent by this transaction (but not by this Split Input).
The Split Input note could be a different unspent note containing the same Asset Base (note that the note will not actually be spent).
The Split Input note could be an already spent note containing the same Asset Base (note that by zeroing the value in the circuit, we prevent double spending).

In the Orchard protocol, since each Action represents an input and an output, the transaction that wants to send one input to multiple outputs must have multiple inputs. The Orchard protocol gives
to the Actions that have not been assigned input notes.
The Orchard technique requires modification for the OrchardZSA protocol with multiple Asset Identifiers, as the output note of the split Actions

Asset Base. We must enforce it to be an actual output of a GroupHash computation (in fact, we want it to be of the same Asset Base as the original input note, but the binding signature takes care that the proper balancing is performed). Without this enforcement the prover could input a multiple (or linear combination) of an existing Asset Base, and thereby attack the network by overflowing the ZEC value balance and hence counterfeiting ZEC funds.
Therefore, for Custom Assets we enforce that

input note to an OrchardZSA Action must be proven to exist in the set of note commitments in the note commitment tree. We then enforce this real note to be “unspendable” in the sense that its value will be zeroed in split Actions and the nullifier will be randomized, making the note not spendable in the specific Action. Then, the proof itself ensures that the output note is of the same Asset Base as the input note. In the circuit, the split note functionality will be activated by a boolean private input to the proof (aka the
boolean). This ensures that the value base points of all output notes of a transfer are actual outputs of a GroupHash, as they originate in the Issuance protocol which is publicly verified.
Note that the Orchard dummy note functionality remains in use for ZEC notes, and the Split Input technique is used in order to support Custom Assets.

Once the transaction version specified by ZIP 248 is allowed on the network, that ZIP requires wallets to be able to parse transactions of that version, and to send only such transactions
. For ZSAs, the corresponding requirements on wallets are:

wallets should switch to sending only the transaction version that supports ZSAs. They should also use the OrchardZSA bundle variant for all of their Ironwood-pool actions, including those that transfer ZEC. The main consequence of not doing so is that users would not otherwise obtain the privacy benefit of indistinguishability between native and non-native assets in the Ironwood shielded pool, because actions in v6 and earlier transactions, and in bundles of other variants, can only transfer the native ZEC asset.

wallets should be ready to receive funds in outputs of the transaction version that supports ZSAs as soon as they activate. The consequence of not doing so would be that funds sent to Orchard-protocol addresses of a wallet without this support could be temporarily inaccessible, until the wallet is upgraded to fully support the relevant transaction version and note plaintext lead byte, and to rescan Ironwood-pool outputs since ZSA activation.
ZIP 248 specifies the digest algorithms for the transaction version that it defines
, and a mechanism for versioning sighash algorithms
. Each bundle type defines its contributions to those digests, and the sighash versions available to its signers together with the associated data that each version requires.
The digests of OrchardZSA bundles, and the sighash versions available to their signers, are yet to be specified.
The fee mechanism for the upgrades proposed in this ZIP will follow the mechanism described in ZIP 317 for the OrchardZSA protocol upgrade, and are described in ZIP 227
In order to have backward compatibility with the ZEC notes, we have designed the circuit to support both ZEC and OrchardZSA notes. As we specify above, there are three main reasons we can do this:
Note commitments for ZEC notes will remain the same, while note commitments for Custom Assets will be computed taking into account the
The Ironwood shielded pool, which already holds Orchard-protocol notes, will also hold the new OrchardZSA-protocol notes after the upgrade.
The value commitment is abstracted to allow for the value base-point as a variable private input to the proof.
The ZEC-based Actions will still include dummy input notes, whereas the OrchardZSA Actions will include split input notes and will not include dummy input notes.
The Zcash Shielded Assets protocol is scheduled to be deployed in Network Upgrade 7 (NU7). This ZIP currently assumes that this will be the case.
